strengths: Comprehensive empirical evaluation comparing multiple RFT and SFT algorithms across seven multimodal tasks with both task-specific and general knowledge benchmarks (MMMU, MMLU-Pro, POPE)
Significant practical finding: RFT achieves forgetting measure of -2.3% compared to SFT's -10.4%, with improvements in general capability preservation
Systematic ablation studies investigating the roles of KL penalty and CoT reasoning, showing neither are primary drivers of forgetting mitigation
Theoretical perspective using Fisher Information Matrix and forgetting risk to explain reward variance as implicit regularization (Proposition 5.2)
Good reproducibility: comprehensive implementation details, promise of code release, clear experimental protocols, and appropriate ethics/reproducibility statements
Well-structured presentation with effective visualizations (especially Figure 1) clearly demonstrating the SFT vs. RFT contrast
weaknesses: Critical methodological concern: SFT uses 10x higher learning rate (1e-5 vs 1e-6) and different batch sizes than RFT, creating unfair comparison where hyperparameter choices rather than paradigm differences may drive results
Theoretical analysis relies on unvalidated Assumption B.2 (Bounded Covariance, Centered Policy Expectation); error term E magnitude never measured, so approximation validity unknown
Limited generalization: single model tested (Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct) with fixed task sequence; unknown if findings hold for other architectures, scales, or task orderings
RIF-RFT proposed method underperforms: achieves worse results than baseline GRPO (57.5% vs 60.0% AvgAcc, -4.5% vs -2.3% FM), contradicting claims of improvement
Instability issue downplayed: GRPO w/o KL requires multiple checkpoint restarts (Table 3), undermining claim that KL is not important for forgetting mitigation
Missing statistical rigor: no error bars, confidence intervals, or significance testing despite small performance differences; some improvements modest (e.g., +2.1% on MMMU)
No comparison to standard continual learning methods (EWC, SI, L2-SP, etc.) even when combined with SFT, limiting context for assessing the contribution
Reward function design is task-specific; generalization to different reward structures unexplored, potentially limiting applicability

strengths: Addresses a relevant problem in continual post-training with comprehensive empirical evaluation across 7 multimodal tasks and general benchmarks (MMMU, MMLU-Pro, POPE)
Thorough ablation studies systematically demonstrate that KL penalty and CoT are not primary mechanisms for forgetting mitigation
Well-designed experimental setup with clear metrics (AvgAcc, FM) and multiple RFT algorithms compared
Clear presentation of main findings with effective visualizations (Figure 1)
Provides reproducibility statement and promises code release
weaknesses: Limited novelty: Core finding that RFT generalizes better than SFT was established by Chu et al. (2025); extension to CPT is incremental

Theoretical analysis (Proposition 5.2) lacks rigor: Assumptions B.2.1 and B.2.2 are never empirically validated, error term E is never measured, and Fisher Information Matrix is acknowledged as 'not computed in practice'
Critical experimental gaps: No comparison with existing CPT methods like LLaVA-c, limiting ability to assess if RFT's advantage persists against sophisticated continual learning strategies
Single model architecture (Qwen2.5-VL-7B), single task sequence order, no statistical significance testing or multiple runs—limited experimental scope

Weak justification for reward variance as primary mechanism: Removing KL doesn't identify variance as the cause; other factors (gradient flow, exploration patterns, loss landscape) could explain stability
RIF-RFT shows underwhelming trade-offs: 4.2% absolute performance drop (60.0% → 57.5% AvgAcc) with worsened forgetting (-2.3% → -4.5% FM) is poorly justified
Critical unexplored findings: GRPO w/o CoT outperforms on VizWiz contradicting intuition; no sensitivity analysis on hand-crafted reward function design
Overclaimed contributions: 'First comprehensive analysis' and 'fundamentally more suitable' are overstated given limited scope; computational overhead of RFT (rollouts) not addressed

strengths: Novel first-of-its-kind comparative analysis of SFT vs. RFT in continual post-training, addressing a fundamental question in foundation model adaptation

Comprehensive experimental evaluation across 7 multimodal tasks with dramatic empirical results (SFT FM: -10.4% vs. GRPO FM: -2.3%), evaluated on both task-specific and general benchmarks (MMMU, MMLU-Pro, POPE)
Rigorous ablation studies effectively demonstrating that KL penalty and CoT are not primary mechanisms, valuable for understanding what doesn't drive forgetting mitigation
Theoretical contribution (Proposition 5.2) linking reward variance to implicit regularization through Fisher Information Matrix analysis, providing intuitive explanation for empirical phenomena
Practical efficiency improvement via RIF-RFT reducing data usage to 48.4% while maintaining competitive knowledge preservation
Strong empirical results showing RFT preserves general capabilities while SFT severely degrades them (SFT: 52.1% → 40.1% on MMMU vs. RFT: 52.1% → 54.2%)
Clear presentation with compelling figures and comprehensive implementation details supporting reproducibility
weaknesses: Severely limited experimental scope: only one base model tested (Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct), only 7 multimodal tasks, only vision-language modality—generalization to other architectures and domains unclear
Theoretical analysis relies on strong unvalidated assumptions (B.2.1, B.2.2) with no empirical verification; error term E = Var[r]δ + ε₁ is unquantified and could be large in practice

Missing critical comparisons with existing continual learning methods (HiDe-LLaVA, MRLoRA, LLaVA-c, Adapt-∞) mentioned in related work, preventing assessment of whether RFT is truly superior or complementary to existing approaches
Inconsistent results across RFT variants on general capabilities: GRPO improves MMMU (+2.1%) while RLOO degrades it (-1.6%), ReMax consistently underperforms, undermining universality claims
No statistical rigor: results appear to be single runs without error bars or confidence intervals; vulnerable to random seed effects; no analysis of task ordering sensitivity

RIF-RFT addresses 'incompetent samples' problem introduced late, suggesting RFT has fundamental limitations not fully resolved; filtering removes 48.4-67.4% of data with performance degradation (57.5% vs. 60.0% AvgAcc)

Incomplete mechanistic analysis: evidence for implicit regularization hypothesis is indirect; could strengthen with direct gradient norm measurements, reward variance tracking during training, and quantitative loss landscape analysis
General capability enhancement claims may be overstated: MMMU improvements modest, MMLU-Pro results mixed across methods, varying between -12.1% degradation (ReMax) and +0.8% improvement (GRPO)

strengths: First systematic comparative investigation of SFT vs RFT paradigms for continual post-training in MLLMs, addressing a previously unexplored fundamental question
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across 7 downstream tasks and 3 general benchmarks (MMMU, MMLU-Pro, POPE) with consistent findings across multiple RFT variants (GRPO, ReMax, RLOO)

Clear and compelling empirical results: RFT achieves near-zero forgetting (FM = -2.3%) while SFT suffers catastrophic forgetting (FM = -10.4%); RFT preserves general capabilities while SFT degrades them by up to 16.9%
Thorough ablation studies effectively ruling out KL penalty and CoT reasoning as primary mechanisms, strengthening the implicit regularization explanation
Theoretical contribution (Proposition 5.2) linking RFT stability to reward variance-scaled updates provides intuitive explanation grounded in continual learning theory
Extensive supplementary experiments validating generalization: text-only tasks, different model scales (3B/8B), task ordering robustness, computational efficiency analysis (44% speedup with RIF-RFT)
Practical algorithm (RIF-RFT) with demonstrated computational benefits without compromising anti-forgetting properties
Strong reproducibility: code provided, comprehensive implementation details, public datasets and models, clear experimental protocol
weaknesses: Theoretical analysis relies on unverified assumptions: Assumption B.2 (Bounded Covariance and Centered Policy Expectation) are never empirically validated; error terms ε₁ and δ in Proposition 5.2 are claimed to be 'small under reasonable conditions' without evidence

Significant experimental confounds: learning rates differ 10-fold (SFT: 1e-5 vs RFT: 1e-6), batch sizes differ dramatically (24 vs 512 rollout batch), making it unclear whether improvements stem from paradigm or hyperparameter choices

Critical ablation result contradicts main claim: GRPO w/o KL requires multiple restarts to converge (Table 3), suggesting KL penalty is essential for practical training, yet paper claims KL is 'not the primary factor' in forgetting mitigation

Limited baseline comparisons: no comparison with recent CPT methods (HiDe-LLaVA, MRLoRA, Adapt-∞, LLaVA-c); only vanilla SFT and one traditional CL baseline (ER in appendix); MTL comparison is confounded as it trains on all data simultaneously

Single-run experiments throughout paper lack statistical rigor: no error bars, confidence intervals, or significance tests; problematic for RL methods with high variance; only Table 9 shows multiple task orderings

Reward function design (Eq. 7) is hand-crafted with arbitrary weights (0.9 accuracy + 0.1 format); sensitivity to reward design choices not evaluated; different downstream tasks may benefit from different weightings

Limited generalization scope: evaluation restricted to vision-language tasks (plus 2 text-only tasks); only Qwen model family tested; unclear if findings hold for other architectures, modalities, or more open-ended generation tasks
RIF-RFT contribution is incremental: simple sample filtering based on non-zero reward; shows notable performance degradation (AvgAcc 60.0% → 57.5%, FM -2.3% → -4.5%); lacks algorithmic novelty

Hyperparameter sensitivity underexplored: KL coefficient β=0.01 not justified; group size=8 not ablated; no sensitivity analysis for SFT/RFT learning rates; only filtering threshold τ studied in ablations

Instability and tradeoffs insufficiently discussed: GRPO w/o KL instability suggests KL importance; GRPO w/o CoT shows hallucination issues; these limitations deserve more prominent treatment in main paper

strengths: Comprehensive experimental evaluation with 7 diverse multimodal tasks, multiple RFT variants, and general benchmarks (MMMU, MMLU-Pro, POPE) demonstrating clear practical differences
Important practical finding that RFT preserves general model capabilities while SFT causes severe degradation, addressing the real base model degradation problem in CPT
Well-designed ablation studies (Tables 3-4) showing CoT and KL penalty are not primary mechanisms, which is counterintuitive and informative
Extensive robustness validation including cross-architecture experiments, model scales (3B, 8B), task ordering variations, and ER baseline comparison in appendix
Reproducibility strengthened by code availability, clear implementation details, use of public benchmarks, and ethics/reproducibility statements
weaknesses: Critical missing baselines: No comparison with state-of-the-art CPT methods (HiDe-LLaVA, MRLoRA, LLaVA-c) mentioned in related work but not evaluated, severely limiting the claims about RFT's superiority

Theoretical contribution (Proposition 5.2) has significant limitations: relies on unverified Assumption B.2 (bounded covariance, centered expectations), provides only an approximation with unknown error term magnitude, and Fisher Information Matrix is never empirically computed, making theory unvalidated

Limited novelty: Core insight that RFT is more stable than SFT is intuitive; uses existing algorithms without methodological innovation; RIF-RFT is a simple filtering heuristic rather than a significant contribution

Scope limitations in main experiments: Single primary model (Qwen2.5-VL-7B) in primary results; 7 specific vision-language tasks; text-only evaluation minimal (only GSM8K→USMLE); reward function design (0.9 accuracy + 0.1 format) appears task-specific without justification

Unresolved tension in key results: Table 3 shows GRPO without KL requires multiple restarts for stability, contradicting the claim that implicit regularization from reward variance is the primary mechanism if explicit KL regularization is necessary for training stability

RIF-RFT performance degradation: Achieves only 57.5% AvgAcc vs. 60.0% for full GRPO (2.5% drop) while filtering 50-60% data but saving only ~44% wall-clock time, making the efficiency-performance trade-off unconvincing
No statistical significance testing: Results lack error bars, confidence intervals, or multiple run reports, making it unclear if differences are statistically robust
Overclaiming in presentation: Terms like 'naturally mitigates,' 'inherent mechanism,' and 'fundamental' overstate findings given the approximate theory and narrow experimental scope

strengths: Comprehensive and rigorous empirical evaluation with multiple RFT algorithms, model scales/architectures, task orderings, and domain robustness tests demonstrating generality

Clear and substantial empirical findings: RFT achieves near-MTL performance (FM: -2.3%) while SFT catastrophically forgets (FM: -10.4%), with stark general capability preservation differences (e.g., MMMU: 52.1%→54.2% vs 52.1%→40.1%)
Systematic ablation studies revealing what is NOT responsible for RFT's stability (KL penalty, CoT), adding nuance beyond the positive findings
Interesting theoretical perspective linking RFT's implicit regularization to reward variance through forgetting risk and Fisher Information (Proposition 5.2)
Practical algorithm (RIF-RFT) with meaningful efficiency gains (~44% speedup) based on principled analysis
Excellent reproducibility: code provided, comprehensive implementation details, public datasets, clear experimental protocols enabling verification
Well-motivated problem of fundamental importance to continual adaptation of foundation models with clear practical deployment implications
weaknesses: Theoretical analysis limitations: Assumption B.2 (Bounded Covariance, Centered Policy Expectation) is stated without empirical validation; error term could be substantial; analysis covers single samples not batch dynamics; actual Fisher Information values never computed; Proposition 5.2 provides intuition rather than rigorous proof

Incomplete causal explanation: Why does SFT degrade general capabilities so severely (↓16.9% even in MTL)? Whether this is fundamental to loss function vs. task specificity vs. reward signal structure remains unclear

Significant gap in baseline comparisons: Related work cites HiDe-LLaVA, MRLoRA, Adapt-∞, LLaVA-c, ModalPrompt, MLLM-CL, and spectral methods designed for CPT, but only Experience Replay is compared (in appendix), not in main results

Fairness of paradigm comparison unclear: RFT uses hand-crafted multi-component reward (0.9·accuracy + 0.1·format) while SFT uses only accuracy; sensitivity to reward weighting unexplored; whether results hold with alternative reward designs unknown

Limited experimental scope: all main experiments on Qwen2.5-VL family only; only 7 vision-language Q&A tasks; text-only domain limited to 2 tasks; would benefit from other architectures (LLaVA, InternVL) and more diverse domains (code, dialogue, reasoning)

Contradictory claims about KL penalty: GRPO w/o KL requires multiple checkpoint restarts for convergence, suggesting KL is important for training stability, yet paper claims KL is 'not the primary factor'—distinction between stability vs. knowledge preservation mechanism is blurred

Statistical rigor gaps: no error bars, confidence intervals, or multi-run reporting; high-variance RFT methods could benefit from uncertainty quantification; significance testing absent despite 7 tasks where noise matters

RIF-RFT performance trade-offs underspecified: degradation from FM -2.3% to -4.5% and AvgAcc 60.0 to 57.5, but limited guidance on when trade-off is worthwhile; validated only on 3B model in main results
Missing critical ablations: sensitivity to reward weighting unexplored; alternative advantage estimators not tested; impact of hyperparameters (rollouts, temperature) on conclusions unclear
